channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: Your personal effort drops when you join a group.
item.description: The phenomenon of decreased group effort is often termed 'social loafing,' a term coined by Latané et al. in 1979, which is historically rooted in the 'Ringelmann effect' documented in 1913.

item.title: You ignore the length of an experience in your memory.
item.description: Duration neglect is a heuristic where the duration of an experience is assigned little weight relative to the emotional 'peak' and 'end' of the event when forming a retrospective evaluation.

item.title: You are blind to the reasons for your own choices.
item.description: Choice blindness is the phenomenon where people fail to notice when their own decisions are manipulated, yet they readily invent reasons for the outcome.

item.title: A final sound can wipe out your last memory.
item.description: The suffix effect is the finding that recall of the final items in a list is inhibited if an irrelevant, spoken sound is presented immediately after the list ends.

item.title: Your feelings dictate your risk assessment before logic starts.
item.description: The affect heuristic is the process of using current emotions to make rapid decisions instead of evaluating complex data.

item.title: You find personal meaning in descriptions written for everyone.
item.description: The Barnum effect is the psychological phenomenon where individuals believe that vague, generic personality descriptions apply specifically to them.

item.title: You naturally remember yourself doing more work than others.
item.description: The egocentric bias leads individuals to claim more responsibility for a collective outcome than they objectively contributed.

item.title: You lose the ability to teach once you learn.
item.description: The curse of knowledge describes the inability to imagine that other people do not know what you know.

item.title: Your mind is trapped by the first number you hear.
item.description: The anchoring effect causes individuals to rely too heavily on the initial piece of information offered when making subsequent judgments.

item.title: You judge the actions of your group more leniently.
item.description: When a member of your own group fails, you attribute it to bad luck; when an outsider fails, you attribute it to their incompetence.

item.title: You are functionally blind for half a second.
item.description: The attentional blink is a performance deficit where individuals struggle to identify a second target in a rapid sequence of stimuli when it appears within 200-500ms of a first target.

item.title: You retain information better when you create it yourself.
item.description: Information generated through your own effort is remembered better than information read or heard passively.

item.title: Simply predicting your behavior makes you more likely to act.
item.description: When people are asked to predict whether they will perform a behavior, they are statistically more likely to perform that behavior later.

item.title: You believe you influenced an outcome that was random.
item.description: When individuals are given a choice in a game of chance, they rate their probability of success as higher than those who were assigned an outcome.

item.title: Negative feedback has twice the impact of positive praise.
item.description: In studies of social interaction and performance, humans weigh negative information significantly more heavily than equivalent positive data.

item.title: Your brain fills in the edges of your vision.
item.description: When shown a photograph, people consistently recall seeing more of the scene than was actually present in the frame.

item.title: You agree to big requests to stay consistent.
item.description: A 1966 study found that people are more likely to accept a large favor if they first agreed to a small one.

item.title: You value items more just because they are rare.
item.description: A 1975 study showed that participants rated cookies as more desirable when they were presented in a nearly empty jar.

item.title: You trust information more when it is easier read.
item.description: A 2008 study found that simple, easy-to-read fonts make statements seem more factual and credible.

item.title: You want to believe that bad things are deserved.
item.description: A 1966 study found that people tend to derogate victims of misfortune to preserve the belief that the world is inherently fair.

item.title: You believe you know others better than they you.
item.description: A 2001 study showed that people consistently rate their understanding of others as superior to the understanding others have of them.

item.title: You sabotage your own work to protect your ego.
item.description: A 1978 study showed that students would rather choose a drug that hinders their performance than risk failing without an excuse.

item.title: You are more likable when you make small mistakes.
item.description: The pratfall effect shows that a blunder increases the attractiveness of a high-competence individual, while the same blunder typically reduces the attractiveness of an average or low-competence individual.

item.title: You fixate on one detail while ignoring the context.
item.description: Focalism is the tendency to focus on a single event when predicting its impact on future well-being while neglecting other aspects of one's life.

item.title: You are most confident when you know the least.
item.description: The 1999 study found that individuals performing in the lowest quartiles of certain tasks significantly overestimate their competence because they lack the metacognitive awareness to recognize their own errors.

item.title: The presence of others decreases your urgency to help.
item.description: The bystander effect reduces the probability of any single individual offering assistance in an emergency when others are present.

item.title: You assume your future self will have your current desires.
item.description: Projection bias is the tendency to overestimate how much your future preferences will align with your present state.

item.title: You are blind to dramatic changes in your environment.
item.description: Change blindness is the failure to notice significant visual alterations during a brief interruption or distraction.

item.title: You remember the intensity of an experience, not duration.
item.description: The peak-end rule explains how you evaluate past events based on their most intense moment and their ending.

item.title: You judge a stranger's intelligence by their physical attractiveness.
item.description: The halo effect is a cognitive bias where one trait influences the overall perception of a person, which Thorndike first observed in workplace/military performance ratings.

item.title: You only remember the very first impression you formed.
item.description: Information presented at the beginning of a sequence is retained better than information in the middle.

item.title: You eventually believe the lies you heard before.
item.description: The persuasive power of a message can increase over time, even if the source was initially discredited.

item.title: You like the people you encounter most frequently.
item.description: Physical proximity is a stronger predictor of friendship than shared interests.

item.title: You spend 47% of your day thinking about nothing.
item.description: A 2010 study found that nearly half of our waking hours are spent thinking about something other than the present task.

item.title: You value your possessions simply because you own them.
item.description: People demand more money to give up an item than they would have paid to acquire it.

item.title: Your performance drops when you fear confirming a stereotype.
item.description: The awareness of a negative stereotype regarding your group can cause an involuntary decline in performance.

item.title: You keep finishing the book you dislike reading.
item.description: The tendency to follow through on an investment is often driven by the cost already incurred.

item.title: Rewards can turn your favorite hobby into a chore.
item.description: Extrinsic incentives often reduce the intrinsic motivation you initially felt for an activity.

item.title: You think your nerves are obvious to everyone around.
item.description: Research shows people overestimate how effectively others read their internal states, a phenomenon known as the illusion of transparency.

item.title: You rate an object higher because you built it.
item.description: The IKEA effect suggests that individuals place a disproportionately high value on products they partially created.

item.title: You ignore information that contradicts your existing world view.
item.description: Confirmation bias is the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information in a way that aligns with your pre-existing beliefs.

item.title: You believe you see the world exactly as it is.
item.description: Naive realism is the human tendency to believe that we see the world objectively while others, who disagree, are biased or misinformed.

item.title: You value a small reward today over a larger one.
item.description: Hyperbolic discounting is the tendency for people to choose smaller, immediate rewards over larger, later rewards as the delay to the larger reward increases.

item.title: You choose the option based on how it is described.
item.description: The framing effect describes how the presentation of information influences your perception of the risks and rewards involved.

item.title: You accept illogical arguments if the conclusion feels true.
item.description: Belief bias is the tendency to judge the strength of an argument based on the believability of its conclusion rather than its logic.

item.title: You are blind to obvious changes in your environment.
item.description: Inattentional blindness occurs when you fail to perceive an unexpected stimulus due to focused attention on another task.

item.title: You claim your successes but blame the environment for failures.
item.description: The self-serving bias describes the pattern of attributing success to internal causes and failure to external causes, though it remains debated whether this is driven by ego-protection or neutral information processing expectancies.

item.title: You remember information best when you connect it to yourself.
item.description: The self-reference effect is the tendency for people to encode information differently when it is related to themselves.

item.title: You judge how common a risk is by how easily you recall it.
item.description: The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut that relies on immediate examples that come to mind when evaluating a topic or decision.

item.title: You remember the core meaning but lose the exact words.
item.description: The verbatim effect states that you are much more likely to remember the meaning of a sentence than the specific words used to express it.
